title: The Educated Barbarian: An introduction to Stoicism (Enchiridion analysis part 3)
summary: Third episode of NH's reading of Epictetus' Enchiridion, covering the folly of wishing loved ones immortal, self-mastery as the only true mastery, the banquet metaphor for desire, sympathy without inner lament, reinterpreting omens, and envy. He ties several passages to lifting: freeing himself from an obsessive relationship with training improved his gains, and he never fails a lift because he only picks battles he can win.
claims: Wishing your loved ones to live forever is foolish: it is outside your control and immortality would be a curse even if you could grant it
Most wild fantasies of 'if I could do this' would end in catastrophe if they came true
Berserk illustrates that granting someone immortality is really sacrificing them for your own enjoyment
Desiring immortality is childish refusal of death; by refusing to die you also refuse to live, since finitude gives life its flavor
Spoiling someone by providing all their needs removes their incentive to live; riches should not be desired for themselves, only the work leading to them is valuable
Lottery winners tend to become miserable because they receive money they did not work for
Anyone manipulated by media or outside forces who cannot think for themselves is a kind of slave, and the population is slowly being pushed toward full servitude
True mastery is mastery of the self; controlling others is only partial mastery and becomes irrelevant once you master yourself
If everyone were master of themselves society would approach a utopia
Desiring something so much that it devours you makes it your master; neediness repels the thing you chase, as with people desperate for love
He was once a slave to lifting: forcing himself to train without enjoyment, feeling obligated and anxious if he missed a day
Most of his lack of physical and spiritual progress was linked to that obsession; after freeing himself from it he made better gains
Stoicism is not mortification: you can still enjoy pleasures, but on your own terms and while staying in control
Grasping desperately for what is out of reach makes you miserable; with patience desired things often come closer on their own
Gods are beings without desire because they can create anything; renouncing desire altogether is akin to enlightenment or nirvana
Polytheist gods like Zeus were representable and partly human, while the monotheist god is impersonal and mysterious
At 27 he does not seek total renunciation but is gradually cutting unnecessary desires from his life
Show sympathy outwardly to someone grieving but do not lament internally; the opinion about the event, not the event, causes sorrow
Unfeeling 'stoics' who tell suffering people to stop suffering are not stoic; a stoic does not push his doctrine onto others
Omens mean what you decide; you can choose to read any sign as positive and the positive mindset makes it so
His family treats the 13th as a lucky day because his grandmother was born on a 13th, flipping a superstition
He never fails a lift because he never picks a weight and rep range that would lead him to fail; pick battles you know you will win
Take only calculated risks; once a risk is outside your control your destiny can slip away
Envying high-status men makes you resent what you most desire and ultimately yourself; hero worship turning to resentment is common and dangerous in teenagers
The jealous man is the one who knows he will never get there; if you stay true to your goal you need not envy anyone
